summary: Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and other women bring spices to Jesus’ tomb, find the great stone rolled away, and find no body inside.
key_insight: The women bought spices for a dead body and worried about who would move the stone. No one was coming to see a risen Lord. Their question on the road shows they expected to find the tomb shut and Jesus inside.
story: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus. {Mk} Other women came with them, bringing the spices they had prepared. {Lk}

Very early on the first day of the week they set out for the tomb. It was still dark when Mary Magdalene went, {Jn} and the day was beginning to dawn; {Mt} they reached the tomb when the sun had risen. {Mk}
On the way they said to one another, “Who will roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?” {Mk}
But when they looked up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, “for it was very large.” {Mk} Mary Magdalene saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. {Jn}
They went in and did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. {Lk}
differences: Matthew names Mary Magdalene and the other Mary; Mark adds Salome; Luke says “certain other women” came too; John names only Mary Magdalene.
John says Mary came “while it was still dark”; Matthew, “as the first day of the week began to dawn”; Mark, “when the sun had risen.”
Matthew says they came “to see the tomb”; Mark and Luke say they brought spices to anoint Him.
Mark says they bought spices when the Sabbath was past; Luke says they brought the spices they had prepared before it (Luke 23:56).
Only Mark records their worry about the stone; only Luke says they went in and found no body.

fit.question: John says Mary Magdalene came “while it was still dark.” Mark says the women came “when the sun had risen.” When did they come?

points.label: Setting out and arriving
points.text: The women likely set out in the dark and reached the tomb as the sun came up. Mark himself joins the two: “Very early in the morning” and “when the sun had risen” (16:2). Matthew’s “began to dawn” covers the same span.

points.label: Mary ahead of the others
points.text: Mary Magdalene may also have gone ahead of the others or turned back sooner, which would explain why John speaks of her alone (see the next event).

fit.note: The writers describe the same early hour from its beginning and from its end. The time of day is not in conflict.
fit.short: The women set out in the dark and arrived as the sun rose; John describes the start, Mark the arrival.

fit.question: Matthew names two women, Mark three, Luke a larger group, and John only Mary Magdalene. How many women came to the tomb?

points.label: Naming some is not saying only
points.text: No writer says only these women came. Luke later names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Mary the mother of James, “and the other women with them” (Luke 24:10). Each writer names those who mattered most to his account.

points.label: Why John names Mary
points.text: John tells Mary Magdalene’s story because he goes on to describe her meeting with the risen Jesus. Even in John her words to Peter hint at others: “we do not know where they have laid Him” (John 20:2).

fit.note: A group of several women, named in part by each writer, explains every account.
fit.short: Several women came; each writer names some. Luke 24:10 lists three and “the other women,” and John follows Mary.

scene.label: After the Sabbath
scene.text: The Sabbath ended at sunset on Saturday. Only then could the women buy spices, and they waited for the first light of Sunday, the first day of the week, to go out to the tomb.

scene.label: Spices for the dead
scene.text: Spices and oils honored the dead and covered the smell of decay. This was not Egyptian embalming; it was a last act of love. Days earlier Jesus had said that Mary of Bethany had “come beforehand to anoint My body for burial” (Mark 14:8).

scene.label: The stone
scene.text: Joseph had rolled the stone into place (Mark 15:46), and Mark says it was very large, too heavy for a few women to move. They say nothing about guards. The guard was set on the Sabbath, and the women may not have known of it.

witnesses.matthew: Matthew says the two Marys came “to see the tomb.” They are the same two women he placed sitting opposite it on Friday evening (27:61), so his witnesses saw both the burial and the empty tomb.
witnesses.mark: Mark gives the women’s worried question and the note that the stone was “very large,” details that read like the memory of someone who was there. Mark names these women at the cross (15:40), at the burial (15:47) and now at the tomb.
witnesses.luke: Luke says they went in and did not find “the body of the Lord Jesus.” In the NKJV this is the only place in the four Gospels where He is called “the Lord Jesus,” a name Luke uses often in Acts.
witnesses.john: John follows Mary Magdalene alone, out “while it was still dark.” John often marks the hour and the dark (3:2; 13:30), and Mary’s story will move from that darkness to meeting the risen Lord face to face.

seeing.reveals: Jesus had kept His word before anyone arrived. The women came to care for a dead body and found that He had no need of their spices.
seeing.living: The women set out though they had no way to move the stone. Their love sent them before the problem was solved, and God had solved it first. Do not wait for every obstacle to be cleared before you go where devotion to Jesus calls you.
seeing.ponder: What stone are you worrying over that God may already have rolled away?

preaching.big_idea: The women came to anoint a dead body, but God had already opened the tomb.
outline: Love that would not stop at the grave (1)
preaching.watch_for: The women’s question in verse 3 has no answer in their world. Mark answers it without naming who moved the stone: it “had been rolled away” (v. 4), the way Scripture often speaks when God is the one acting.

title: The Women Come to the Tomb
